newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany won't meet EMU criteria - top institute.
newsitem.headline: Germany won't meet EMU criteria - top institute.

text.p: Germany will this year fail to meet the Maastricht Treaty deficit and debt criteria which are crucial for joining Europe's single currency, a top German economist said on Friday.

Heiner Flassbeck, chief economist at the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), told Reuters Financial Television: "In our opinion the (German) government won't meet the fiscal criteria this year, but it will meet the stability criteria."
EU states will be judged on their ability to take part in Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) on the basis of 1997 data.
While Germany is widely expected to meet requirements on exchange rate and price stability without difficulty, the Maastricht targets for debt and deficit levels are viewed as more problematic.
Flassbeck said the Berlin institute expects Germany to exceed the Maastricht reference level for budget deficits -- three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- by 0.5 percentage points.
"Also, government debt will be slightly above 60 percent," Flassbeck added. The Maastricht treaty describes 60 percent debt of GDP as the critical threshold.
But Flassbeck said he was confident that European Monetary Union (EMU) would go ahead on time anyway.
"Three percent and 60 percent aren't the Maastricht criteria as such, but the German interpretation of the Maastricht criteria," he said.

"It is a very open question, whether the other (countries) will follow Germany in this strict interpretation," Flassbeck said, referring to the treaty's provision that a pronounced and lasting development towards the debt and deficit targets is sufficient to qualify.

Flassbeck also said the institute remained pessimistic about Germany's growth potential and saw no reason to change its forecast from January, when the DIW predicted two percent growth this year for Germany as a whole, and only one percent growth in the eastern states.
Aside from exports, Flassbeck said he could not detect any growth engines that could possibly boost German GDP.

Private consumption was weak and would stay that way. Private investment might accelerate a little bit over the course of this year, but not enough to have a significant impact on the overall economy, he said.
